questions.stem: James, 26, has had a daily pressing headache for 6 weeks and keeps rubbing his stiff, sore neck. He is afebrile. While examining him in general practice, you want to show the examiner you have assessed for meningism. Which examination finding best argues against meningeal irritation?
options: Tenderness on palpation of the trapezius and suboccipital muscles
Full, painless passive neck flexion bringing the chin to the chest
Pain-free active neck rotation through a full range to both sides
Normal power, tone and reflexes in all four limbs
questions.why: Meningeal irritation mainly limits and makes painful passive neck flexion, because flexion stretches the inflamed meninges. Full, painless passive flexion (with a negative Kernig's sign) separates muscular stiffness from meningism.
notes: Pericranial muscle tenderness supports tension-type headache, but finding it does not exclude meningeal irritation as well.
Meningism usually leaves rotation relatively spared, so a full range of rotation does not rule it out.
A normal limb neurological examination looks for focal deficits, not meningeal irritation.

questions.stem: James, 26, has tension-type headache with a normal examination. He takes paracetamol 1 g on about 5 days a week and adds ibuprofen 400 mg once or twice a week (no asthma reaction). Along with non-drug measures, what is the most appropriate advice about acute analgesia?
options: Paracetamol 1 g four times daily, regularly, to stop the headaches building up
Paracetamol-codeine 500/30 mg, two tablets, on days when paracetamol alone fails
Paracetamol 1 g or ibuprofen 400 mg early in a headache, on fewer than 10 days a month
Stop all analgesics abruptly today and start amitriptyline 10 mg at night instead
questions.why: Simple analgesia (paracetamol 1 g or ibuprofen 400 mg) taken early works for acute tension-type headache. Keep it to fewer than 10 days a month (about 2 days a week) to prevent medication-overuse headache.
notes: Regular daily analgesia is the exact pattern that leads to medication-overuse headache.
Codeine is no more effective for tension-type headache and carries a higher risk of medication-overuse headache and dependence, so avoid it.
He does not yet have medication-overuse headache, so abrupt withdrawal is not needed. Prophylaxis is considered at review only if headaches stay frequent after non-drug measures.

questions.stem: James, 26, has taken analgesics on about 20 to 25 days a month for 6 weeks for tension-type headache. You warn him that if this continues he will develop medication-overuse headache. Which mechanism best explains how frequent analgesic use makes headache worse?
options: Central sensitisation of trigeminal pain pathways, lowering the pain threshold
Rebound cerebral vasodilation each time a paracetamol dose wears off
Build-up of a toxic paracetamol metabolite causing low-grade encephalopathy
NSAID-induced fluid retention gradually raising intracranial pressure
questions.why: Repeated analgesic exposure is thought to change central pain processing, sensitising trigeminal nociceptive neurones and weakening descending pain inhibition. The threshold drops and headaches become more frequent.
notes: Rebound vasodilation has been proposed for ergotamine, not simple analgesics, and it does not explain medication-overuse headache from paracetamol.
Therapeutic doses of paracetamol do not cause encephalopathy. Its toxic metabolite NAPQI matters in overdose and harms the liver, not the brain.
Occasional ibuprofen does not raise intracranial pressure, and medication-overuse headache also happens with paracetamol alone.

questions.stem: On fundoscopy, James, 26, has sharp optic disc margins with spontaneous venous pulsations, which argues against raised intracranial pressure as the cause of his 6 weeks of daily headache. Which anatomical feature explains why raised intracranial pressure would cause papilloedema?
options: The optic nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure beside the cavernous sinus
The optic nerve is supplied within the orbit by the posterior cerebral artery
Optic nerve fibres are myelinated by Schwann cells, which swell under pressure
The optic nerve sheath has a subarachnoid space continuous with the intracranial one
questions.why: The optic nerve is wrapped in meninges, and its subarachnoid space is continuous with the intracranial one. Raised CSF pressure therefore travels along the sheath to the disc, blocking axoplasmic flow and venous return, which swells the disc and abolishes venous pulsations.
notes: The optic nerve enters through the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.
The orbital optic nerve is supplied by branches of the ophthalmic artery (from the internal carotid), not the posterior cerebral artery.
The optic nerve is a CNS tract myelinated by oligodendrocytes, and myelin swelling is not how papilloedema develops.
